reason: The provided sources offer rich, cross-verified accounts detailing the 1944 West Loch explosion, its immediate cover-up, casualties, and long-term military safety reforms.
story: On May 21, 1944, twenty-nine Landing Ships, Tank (LSTs) were packed beam-to-beam at West Loch in Pearl Harbor, preparing for the top-secret invasion of Saipan. The vessels were floating powder kegs, loaded with thousands of gallons of high-octane fuel and ammunition. At 3:08 p.m., an explosion ripped through the bow of LST-353 during mortar unloading. Within minutes, raining debris ignited gasoline drums on neighboring ships, triggering a catastrophic chain reaction of fires and mushrooming blasts. Over 20 buildings on shore were damaged, and six LSTs sank. Officially, 163 servicemen died and 396 were wounded, with over a third of the casualties coming from the Army's segregated 29th Chemical Decontamination Company. Fearing Japanese awareness of the invasion, military authorities enforced a strict press blackout and classified the tragedy until 1960. Remarkably, the invasion fleet sailed just one day late.
angle: A catastrophic explosion at Pearl Harbor killed 163 men and destroyed six invasion ships right before a secret Pacific assault, but the military covered it up for decades.

claims.claim: On May 21, 1944, at 3:08 p.m., an explosion aboard LST-353 initiated the West Loch disaster.

evidence.quote: On May 21, 1944, at 3:08 p.m., an explosion blossomed out of LST-353.
at 3:08 p.m. something caused an explosion aboard LST-353 near its bow.

claims.claim: Official military records list 163 men killed and 396 wounded in the disaster.

evidence.quote: Dead were 163 men and 396 were wounded.
Official casualty figures list 163 dead and 396 wounded.

claims.claim: Six Landing Ships, Tank (LSTs) were completely sunk or destroyed during the incident.

evidence.quote: In all six LSTs were sunk
Six LSTs sank completely.

claims.claim: Twenty-nine LSTs were moored closely together across six berths in West Loch while preparing for the invasion of the Marianas.

evidence.quote: 29 LSTs readied for the invasion of Saipan, were nestled together at six berths.
Twenty-nine ships moored beam-to-beam at six berths.

claims.claim: High-octane gasoline drums were stored directly on the exposed forecastles and decks of the LSTs.

evidence.quote: To aid quick deployment once ashore, high-octane gasoline was stored in barrels on deck.
Each vessel carried 80 to 100 drums of high-octane fuel on forecastle.

claims.claim: Army troops were unloading mortar ammunition immediately prior to the first blast.

evidence.quote: immediately prior to the explosion, Army stevedores were unloading mortar ammunition
where Army troops had been unloading mortar ammunition.

claims.claim: Four days after the explosion, authorities issued only a single-paragraph statement acknowledging limited damage and loss of life.

evidence.quote: Four days after the incident, the authorities released a one-paragraph statement noting an explosion had caused "some loss of life, a number of injuries and resulted in the destruction of several small vessels".

Four days after the incident, officials released a notice acknowledging an explosion had occurred causing “some loss of life, a number of injuries and resulted in the destruction of several small vessels.”

claims.claim: Details of the disaster remained classified by the U.S. military until 1960.

evidence.quote: The disaster was classified until 1960 and is therefore not well known.
The classification remained until 1960.

claims.claim: The invasion fleet departed Pearl Harbor for the Marianas campaign only one day behind schedule.

evidence.quote: only a day was lost in the departure of the invasion fleet.
The invasion fleet departed Pearl Harbor only one day behind schedule.

claims.claim: Navy diver Francis P. Hammerberg was posthumously awarded the Medal of Honor, becoming the last person to receive it for a non-combat action.

evidence.quote: He was the only service member in World War II, and the last person of all, to receive the Medal of Honor for a non-combat action.
He became the only World War II service member to receive the medal for a noncombat action.

claims.claim: The West Loch disaster and the Port Chicago explosion two months later led to major changes in U.S. Navy ordnance-handling procedures.

evidence.quote: The incident – together with the Port Chicago disaster two months later – led to major changes in weapons-handling practices within the United States Navy.
The West Loch and Port Chicago disasters led the Navy to change the way it handled munitions

claims.claim: About one-third of the casualties belonged to the Army's segregated 29th Chemical Decontamination Company.

evidence.quote: Nearly one-third of the 163 documented and confirmed casualties came from the 29th Chemical Decontamination Company.
About a third of the casualties that day were Black soldiers with the Army’s segregated 29th Chemical Decontamination Company.

claims.claim: The rusting bow of LST-480 remains visible in West Loch.

evidence.quote: the bow of LST-480 is visible as it rusts in the tropical air of Oahu.
Only LST-480's rusting bow remains visible in West Loch.

claims.claim: Gravestones for unidentified victims at the National Memorial Cemetery of the Pacific were updated to specify the West Loch disaster.

evidence.quote: The markers now read "Unknown, West Loch Disaster, May 21, 1944."
The headstones were originally marked simply “Unknown” but have since been updated with the inscription “Unknown, West Loch Disaster, May 21, 1944.”

disputed: Total death toll: Official records state 163 died, but magazine articles and survivor accounts estimate losses between 392 and over 1,000 or 2,000 due to chaotic record-keeping for Army and Marine personnel. The script should cite the official figure of 163 while noting higher estimates exist according to researchers.

Exact cause of initial explosion aboard LST-353: Naval inquiries could not determine whether an dropped 4.2-inch mortar shell or ignition of high-octane gasoline vapors from welding or smoking caused the blast. The script should frame both possibilities as unproven theories.

Japanese midget submarine recovery: Some marine researchers hypothesize that salvage operations clearing West Loch after the disaster recovered the fifth Japanese midget submarine from the 1941 Pearl Harbor attack and dumped it offshore. The script should attribute this as a working theory among marine forensic historians.
